Here the proposition needs proof; for it is not evident, nor does it stand fast among all men, because many think that philosophy is of no benefit, and very many even that it is harmful. The assumption is evident; for it is this: "But one ought to wish to be wise." Because this is perceived of itself and is understood to be true, it is of no use to prove it. Therefore the argument must at once be concluded. There is, then, a certain assumption which does not need proof; for that a certain one does need it is evident. The proof, then, is separate from the assumption. It is false, therefore, that the argument is no more than threefold.

66. And from these things this is now evident: that there is a certain argument in which neither the proposition nor the assumption needs proof—of this kind, to set down something definite and brief by way of example: "If wisdom is to be sought above all, folly is to be avoided above all; but wisdom is to be sought above all; therefore folly is to be avoided above all." Here both the proposition and the assumption are evident; therefore neither needs proof. From all these things this is evident: that the proof is sometimes added and sometimes not added. From which it is recognized that the proof is contained neither in the proposition nor in the assumption, but that each, set in its proper place, holds its own force as something fixed and proper to it. But if this is so, they have divided rightly who have distributed the argument into five parts.

67. There are, then, five parts of that argument which is handled by reasoning: the proposition, by which that topic is briefly set forth from which all the force of the reasoning ought to flow; the proof, by which what has been briefly set forth, confirmed by reasons, is made more probable and clearer; the assumption, by which that which, drawn from the proposition, serves to demonstrate the point, is assumed; the proof of the assumption, by which what has been assumed is confirmed by reasons; the conclusion, by which what is gathered from the whole argument is briefly set forth. The argument which has the most parts consists of these five parts; the second has four parts; the third, three; then there is one of two parts; which is in dispute.

68. As to whether it can consist of even a single part, it may seem possible to someone. Of those, then, which are settled we shall set down examples; of those which are doubtful we shall bring forward reasons. The five-part argument is of this kind: "All laws, judges, ought to be referred to the advantage of the commonwealth, and they ought to be interpreted according to the common benefit, not according to the letter that is in the writing. For our ancestors were of such virtue and wisdom that, in writing the laws, they proposed to themselves nothing else but the safety and advantage of the commonwealth. For they did not themselves wish to write what would be harmful, and, if they had written it, they understood that, once it was perceived, the law would be repudiated. For no one wishes the laws to be preserved for the sake of the laws, but for the sake of the commonwealth, since all think the commonwealth best administered by the laws. Therefore, for the very reason that the laws ought to be observed, it is fitting that all that is written should be interpreted toward that end: that is, since we serve the commonwealth, let us interpret according to the advantage and benefit of the commonwealth. For as one ought to think that nothing proceeds from medicine except what looks to the advantage of the body, since for its sake it was established, so one should judge that nothing proceeds from the laws except what is conducive to the commonwealth, since for its sake they were framed.

69. Therefore in this trial too cease to scrutinize the letter of the law, and consider the law, as is just, according to the advantage of the commonwealth. What was more advantageous to the Thebans than that the Spartans should be crushed? For whom was it more fitting that Epaminondas, the general of the Thebans, should take thought than for the victory of the Thebans? What was it fitting for him to hold dearer or more precious than the great glory of the Thebans, than so bright and adorned a trophy? Was he, forsooth, to neglect the letter of the law and consider the framer's intent? But this surely has been sufficiently considered: that there is no law which has not been written for the sake of the commonwealth. He thought it, therefore, the greatest madness that what had been written for the sake of the safety of the commonwealth should not be interpreted according to the safety of the commonwealth. But if it is fitting that all laws be referred to the advantage of the commonwealth, and this man benefited the safety of the commonwealth, surely he cannot by the same deed both have looked to the common fortunes and have failed to obey the laws."

70. An argument consists of four parts when we either propose or assume without a proof. This one ought to do when either the proposition is understood of itself, or the assumption is evident and needs no proof. With the proof of the proposition passed over, the argument is handled in four parts, in this manner: "Judges, you who judge under oath according to the law, ought to obey the laws. But you cannot obey the laws unless you follow what is written in the law. For what surer testimony of his intent could the framer of the law leave than that which he himself wrote with great care and diligence? But if the writing did not exist, we should greatly require it, that from it the framer's intent might be known; nor yet would we permit Epaminondas, not even if he were outside the court, to interpret for us the intent of the law—much less now should we suffer this man, when the law is at hand, to interpret the framer's intent, not from what is written most plainly, but from what suits his own cause. But if you, judges, ought to obey the laws, and cannot do this unless you follow what is written in the law, why do you not judge that this man has acted against the law?"

71. But with the proof of the assumption passed over, the four-part argument will be made thus: "Those who have time and again deceived us through trust ought not to have their word believed. For if we suffer any harm through their treachery, there will be no one but ourselves whom we can rightly accuse. And to be deceived once is unfortunate; a second time, foolish; a third time, disgraceful. But the Carthaginians have very often by now deceived us. It is therefore the greatest madness to place hope in the trustworthiness of those by whose treachery you have so often been deceived."

72. With both proofs passed over, it becomes three-part, in this way: "Either we must fear the Carthaginians, if we leave them unharmed, or we must destroy their city. But fear them indeed we ought not. It remains, then, that we destroy their city." There are, however, those who think that sometimes the conclusion can be dispensed with, when what is inferred from the reasoning is evident; and that, if this be done, the argument becomes two-part as well, in this manner: "If she has given birth, she is not a virgin; but she has given birth." Here it is enough to propose and to assume: since what is inferred is evident, the matter does not need a conclusion. But to us it seems that every reasoning ought to be concluded, and that the fault which displeases those men should be greatly avoided—namely, that we should not bring into the conclusion what is evident.

73. And this can be done if the kinds of conclusions are understood. For we shall either conclude by drawing the proposition and assumption together into one, in this manner: "But if it is fitting that all laws be referred to the advantage of the commonwealth, and this man benefited the safety of the commonwealth, surely he cannot by the same deed both have looked to the common safety and have failed to obey the laws"; or so that the sense is inferred from the contrary, in this manner: "It is therefore the greatest madness to place hope in the trustworthiness of those by whose treachery you have so often been deceived"; or so that only what is inferred is brought in, in this manner: "Let us therefore destroy the city"; or so that what necessarily follows that which is inferred is brought in. This is of the following kind: "If she has given birth, she has lain with a man; but she has given birth." This is inferred: "She has therefore lain with a man." If you do not wish to bring this in, and instead bring in what follows—"She has therefore committed incest"—you will both have concluded the argument and have avoided the evident conclusion.

74. Therefore in long arguments one ought to conclude by drawings-together or by the contrary, in short ones to set forth only what is inferred, and in those in which the outcome is evident to use the consequence. But if some shall think that an argument can consist of even a single part, they will be able to say that it is often enough to make an argument in this manner: "Since she has given birth, she has lain with a man"; for this, they say, needs neither proof nor conclusion. But to us they seem to err through the ambiguity of the term. For the word "argument" signifies two things, since both something probable or necessary discovered with reference to some matter is called an argument, and the artful working-out of that discovery is so called.

75. When, therefore, they bring forward something of this kind—"Since she has given birth, she has lain with a man"—they bring forward a discovery, not a working-out; but we are speaking of the parts of the working-out. That reasoning, therefore, will have nothing to do with this matter; and by this distinction we shall repel the other objections too which will seem to stand in the way of this division, if anyone should think that sometimes the assumption can be removed, or the proposition. For these, if they have anything probable or necessary, must in some way move the hearer. But if only this were regarded, and it made no difference how that which had been devised was handled, then it would by no means be thought that there is so great a difference between the highest orators and the mediocre.

76. But it will be very necessary to vary the speech; for in all things sameness is the mother of satiety. This can be done if we do not always enter upon the argument in the same way. For, first of all, it is fitting to make distinctions by the very kinds—that is, to use now induction, now reasoning; then, in the argument itself, not always to begin from the proposition, nor always to make use of all five parts, nor to polish the parts in the same way; but now to begin from the assumption, now from one or the other proof, now from both, now to use this, now that, kind of conclusion. That this may be perceived, let us write—on any example of those which have been set forth—how easy it is to do; one may make the trial.

77. And about the parts of an argument enough seems to have been said by us; but we wish it understood that we know well that arguments are also handled in philosophy by many other methods, and obscure ones, about which there is an established and definite system; but these seemed to us to be foreign to oratorical use. As for those things which we think pertain to speaking, we do not affirm that we have attended to them more conveniently than others; we do promise that we have written them up more thoroughly and carefully. Now, as we have determined, we shall proceed in order to the rest.

78. The refutation is that by which, by arguing, the confirmation of our opponents is dissolved or weakened. This will use the same source of invention which the confirmation uses, for the reason that from the same topics from which any matter can be confirmed, from those same topics it can be invalidated. For nothing is to be considered in all these except that which is assigned to persons or to actions. Therefore the invention and the working-out of arguments must be transferred to this part of the speech too from those things which have been taught before. Nevertheless, that some instruction may be given for this part as well, we shall set forth the modes of refutation; and those who observe them will be able more easily to dissolve or weaken the things that are said against them.

79. Every argument is refuted if either something—one thing or several—of those things which have been taken is not granted, or, when these are granted, the conclusion is denied to follow from them, or if the very kind of the argument is shown to be faulty, or if against a firm argument another, equally firm or firmer, is set. Something of those things which are taken is not granted, when either what they call credible is denied to be of that kind, or what they think comparable is shown to be dissimilar, or a precedent is turned to the other side, or the judgment is altogether disapproved, or what our opponents have said to be a sign is denied to be of that kind, or a dilemma is refuted either on one side or on both, or an enumeration is shown to be false, or a simple inference is demonstrated to contain something false. For everything that is taken for arguing, whether as probable or as necessary, must necessarily be taken from these topics, as we have shown before.

80. What has been taken as credible will be weakened if either it is plainly false, in this manner: "There is no one who would not prefer money to wisdom"; or it has something credible from the contrary side too, in this manner: "Who is there who is not more eager for duty than for money?"; or it is altogether incredible, as if someone who is agreed to be greedy should say that he had neglected the greatest sum of money for the sake of some moderate duty; or if what happens in certain matters or persons is said to befall all, in this way: "Those who are poor hold money dearer than duty; in a place which is deserted, a murder must have been committed; how could a man have been killed in a frequented place?"; or if what rarely happens is denied to happen at all, as Curio for Fulvius: "No one can fall in love at a single glance, nor in passing by."

81. What is taken as a sign will be weakened from the same topics from which it is confirmed. For in a sign it must first be shown to be true; then to be a sign proper to the matter under discussion, as blood to a murder; then that what ought not to have been done was done, or what ought to have been done was not done; finally, that the person under inquiry knew the law and custom of that matter. For these are the things assigned to a sign; which we shall open up more carefully when we speak separately of the conjectural issue itself. Therefore each one of these will, in refutation, be shown either not to be a sign, or to be too slight a one, or to stand for our side rather than our opponents', or to be stated altogether falsely, or to be capable of being drawn to another suspicion too.

82. But when something is introduced as comparable, since it is handled chiefly by likeness, in refuting it will be fitting to deny that what is compared is like that with which it is compared. This can be done if it is shown to be different in kind, nature, force, magnitude, time, place, person, or opinion; and if it is shown in what class that which is brought forward by likeness, and in what class this for the sake of which it is brought forward, ought to be reckoned. Then we shall show in what one matter differs from the other; from which we shall teach that one ought to judge differently about that which is compared and about that with which it is compared. Of this faculty we have most need when the very argument which is handled by induction is to be refuted. But if some precedent is brought in, since it is confirmed chiefly from these topics—the praise of those who judged; the likeness of the matter under discussion to that about which judgment was given; and by mentioning that the judgment was not only not blamed but approved by all; and by showing that what is brought forward was more difficult and important to judge than what is now at issue—it will be necessary to weaken it from the contrary topics, if the matter, true or probable, allows. And it will be necessary to observe carefully that what was judged has nothing to do with the matter at issue; and we must see that the matter not be brought forward in which there was offence, so that judgment may seem to be passed on the very man who judged.

83. But one must take care that, when many things have been judged otherwise, some solitary or rare judgment not be brought forward. For thus, by these means, the authority of a judgment can most be weakened. And these things, indeed, which are taken as probable, ought to be tried in this manner. But those things which are stated as necessary, if perhaps they merely imitate a necessary argument and are not really of that kind, will be refuted thus. First, the dilemma, which, whichever you grant, ought to confute you: if it is true, it will never be refuted; but if false, in two ways, either by conversion or by the invalidation of one of its parts, in this manner: "For if he is modest, why do you accuse one who is upright? But if he possesses a shameless cast of mind, why do you accuse one who esteems being so charged of little account?" Here, whether you say he is modest or not modest, he thinks it must be granted that you deny he should be accused. This is refuted by conversion thus: "Nay rather, he must be accused. For if he is modest, you may accuse him; for he will not esteem being so charged of little account. But if he possesses a shameless cast of mind, you may still accuse him; for he is not upright."

84. But by the invalidation of one part it will be refuted in this manner: "But if he is modest, corrected by your accusation he will withdraw from his error." An enumeration is recognized as faulty if we either state something passed over which we should be willing to grant, or something weak is numbered in which can either be denied or for which there is no reason why we cannot honourably grant it. Something is passed over in enumerations of this kind: "Since you have that horse, either you must have bought it, or you possess it by inheritance, or you received it as a gift, or it was born to you at home, or, if none of these is the case, you must have stolen it: if you neither bought it, nor did it come by inheritance, nor was it given, nor born at home—you must therefore have stolen it."

85. This is conveniently refuted if it can be said that the horse was captured from the enemy, the sale of which booty was not held; and when this is brought in, the enumeration is weakened, since that has been introduced which was passed over in the enumeration. But in the other way it will be refuted if either something is said on the contrary—that is, if, for the sake of example, to keep to the same case, it can be shown that it came by inheritance—or if that last item is not disgraceful to grant; as if someone, when his opponents have said, "You either wished to lay an ambush, or you complied with a friend, or you were carried away by desire," should confess that he complied with a friend.

86. A simple inference is refuted if what follows does not seem necessarily to cohere with what preceded. For this: "If he draws breath, he lives; if it is day, it is light," is of such a kind that the latter seems necessarily to cohere with the former. But this: "If she is a mother, she loves; if she once erred, she will never be corrected," will fittingly be refuted in such a way that it is shown that the latter does not necessarily cohere with the former. This kind, and the other necessary kinds, and in general every argument and its refutation, contains a certain greater force and extends more widely than is here set forth; but the knowledge of that art is of such a kind that it cannot be joined to some part of this art, but itself requires, separately, a long time and a great and arduous study. Therefore those matters will be explained by us at another time and for another purpose, if there be opportunity; now it will be necessary for us to be content with these precepts of the rhetoricians, for oratorical use. When, therefore, something of those things which are taken is not granted, it will be weakened thus.

87. But when, these being granted, the conclusion is not made from them, these things will have to be considered: whether something other is concluded than is stated, in this manner: if, when someone says that he set out for the army, another should wish to use against him this argument: "If you had come to the army, you would have been seen by the military tribunes; but you were not seen by them; you did not, therefore, set out for the army." Here, when you have granted the proposition and the assumption, the conclusion is to be weakened.

88. For something other has been inferred than was being forced. And now, that the matter might be more easily understood, we have set down an example endowed with a plain and gross fault; but often a fault more obscurely placed is approved as true, when either you remember too little what you have granted, or you have granted something ambiguous as certain. If you have granted something ambiguous in the sense in which you yourself understood it, and your opponent should wish to adapt it to another sense through the conclusion, it will be necessary to show that the conclusion is made not from what you yourself granted, but from what he assumed, in this manner: "If you need money, you do not have money; if you do not have money, you are poor; but you need money—for otherwise you would not give your effort to trade; therefore you are poor." This is refuted thus: "When you said, 'If you need money, you do not have money,' I understood this: 'If through want you are in destitution, you do not have money,' and therefore I granted it; but when you assumed this, 'But you need money,' I took it as, 'But you wish to have more money.' From which concessions this is not inferred: 'You are therefore poor'; but it would be inferred if I had first granted you this too, that whoever wished to have more money does not have money."

89. But often they think you have forgotten what you have granted, and therefore that which is not inferred is brought into the conclusion as though it were inferred, in this manner: "If the inheritance was coming to him, it is probable that he was killed by him." Then they prove this in very many words. Afterwards they assume: "But the inheritance was coming to him." Then it is inferred: "He, therefore, killed him"; which from the things they had taken is not inferred. Therefore one must observe carefully both what is taken and what is inferred from these. But the very kind of the argument will be shown to be faulty for these reasons: if either there is a fault in it itself, or it is not adapted to the point that is undertaken. And there will be a fault in itself if it is wholly false, if it is common, if vulgar, if trifling, if far-fetched, if it has a bad definition, if it is controversial, if evident, if not granted, if disgraceful, if offensive, if contrary, if inconsistent, if self-opposing.

90. It is false in which there is a plain lie, in this manner: "He cannot be wise who neglects money; but Socrates neglected money; therefore he was not wise." It is common which makes no more for our opponents than for us, in this manner: "Therefore, judges, because I had a true case, I pleaded briefly." It is vulgar which, if it were now granted, could be transferred to another improbable matter too, as this: "If he did not have a true case, he would not have entrusted himself to you, judges." It is trifling which is either spoken after the time, in this manner: "If it had come into his mind, he would not have done it"; or which wishes to cover a plainly disgraceful matter with a slight defence, in this manner: "When all sought you out, while your kingdom flourished, I left you; now, when you are deserted by all, in the greatest danger, I alone prepare to restore you."

91. It is far-fetched which is sought further than is enough, of this kind: "But if Publius Scipio had not bestowed his daughter Cornelia upon Tiberius Gracchus, and begotten the two Gracchi from her, such great seditions would not have arisen; therefore this misfortune seems to be ascribed to Scipio." Of this kind is that lament too: "Would that the fir-beams, felled by axes in the Pelian grove, had not fallen to the ground!"—for it is fetched further back than the matter demanded. The definition is bad when it either describes things common, in this manner: "A seditious man is one who is a bad and useless citizen"—for this describes the force of a seditious man no more than of an ambitious one, of a slanderer, of any wicked man—; or states something false, in this way: "Wisdom is the understanding of how to acquire money"; or contains something neither weighty nor great, thus: "Folly is an immense desire for glory." This is indeed folly, but defined in some one part, not in its whole kind. It is controversial in which, to demonstrate something doubtful, a doubtful cause is brought forward, in this manner: "Ho, you gods, who have the power of stirring the things above and below, do you reconcile peace among yourselves and bring concord together?"

92. It is evident about which there is no controversy: as if someone, when he accuses Orestes, should make it plain that the mother was killed by him. It is not granted when that which is being magnified is in controversy, as if someone, when he accuses Ulysses, should dwell most on this: that it was unworthy that Ajax, a most brave man, was killed by a most cowardly man. It is disgraceful which seems unworthy on account of some dishonourable matter, either by the place in which it is said, or by the man who says it, or by the time at which it is said, or by those who hear, or by the matter under discussion. It is offensive which wounds the will of those who hear: as if someone, before Roman knights eager to be judges, should praise the judiciary law of Caepio.

93. It is contrary which is said contrary to what those who hear have done: as if someone, speaking before Alexander of Macedon against some stormer of cities, should say that there is nothing more cruel than to destroy cities, when Alexander himself had destroyed Thebes. It is inconsistent which is said differently by the same man about the same matter: as if someone, having said that he who has virtue needs nothing for living well, should afterwards deny that one can live well without good health; or that he stands by a friend out of good will, but hopes that some advantage will come to himself.

94. It is self-opposing which in some part stands in the way of the very cause, as if someone should magnify the force, the resources, and the good fortune of the enemy when he is exhorting the soldiers to fight. If some part of the argument is not adapted to the point undertaken, it will be found in one of these faults: if, having promised more, one demonstrates fewer; or if, when one ought to show the whole, one speaks of some part, in this manner: "The race of women is greedy; for Eriphyle sold her husband's life for gold"; or if one does not defend that which is being accused, as if someone, when he is accused of bribery, should defend himself as being strong of hand; or as Amphion in Euripides, who, having reviled music, praises wisdom; or if a matter is reviled on account of a man's fault, as if someone should blame learning on account of the faults of some learned man; or if someone, when he wishes to praise a man, speaks of his good fortune, not of his virtue; or if one so compares one matter with another that he does not think he praises the one unless he reviles the other;

95. or if he so praises the one that he makes no mention of the other; or if, when the inquiry is about a definite matter, the speech is framed about the general, as if someone, when certain men are deliberating whether they should wage a war or not, should praise peace altogether, instead of demonstrating that that particular war is inexpedient; or if a false reason for some matter is given, in this manner: "Money is a good thing, for the reason that it most of all makes life happy"; or a weak one, as Plautus: "To chastise a friend for a deserved fault is a thankless deed; but in the course of life it is useful and profitable; for I shall today soundly chastise my friend for a fault he has deserved"; or the same reason, in this manner: "Avarice is an evil; for the desire of money has afflicted many with great misfortunes"; or one too little suited, in this manner: "The greatest good is friendship; for there are very many delights in friendship."

96. The fourth mode of refutation was that by which, against a firm argument, one equally firm or firmer is set. This kind will be employed chiefly in deliberations, when we grant that something said on the contrary side is fair, but demonstrate that what we defend is necessary; or when we admit that what they defend is useful, but demonstrate that what we say is honourable. And these are the things we have thought ought to be said about refutation.

97. Hermagoras next places digression, then the final conclusion. In this digression he thinks one ought to introduce a passage removed from the cause and from the point for decision itself, which contains either praise of oneself or blame of one's opponent, or leads off into another cause, from which he draws some confirmation or refutation, not by arguing but by amplifying through a kind of enlargement. If anyone thinks this is a part of the speech, he may follow him. But it has not pleased us to count it in, because we are displeased to digress from the cause except through a commonplace; about which kind we must speak later. As for praises and blames, it pleases us that they be treated not separately, but be interwoven in the arguments themselves. Now we shall speak about the conclusion.

98. The conclusion is the close and finishing of the whole speech. It has three parts: the recapitulation, the indignation (rousing of resentment), and the appeal to pity. The recapitulation is that by which matters scattered and diffusely stated are gathered into one place and, for the sake of remembrance, brought under one view. If this is always handled in the same way, it will be plainly understood by all to be handled by a certain artifice; but if it is done in various ways, it will be able to avoid both this suspicion and satiety. Therefore one ought sometimes to do as most do, on account of its ease—to touch upon each single matter and so to pass briefly over all the arguments; and sometimes—which is more difficult—to state what parts you have set forth in the partition, of which you promised to speak, and to bring back to memory by what reasons you have confirmed each several part; and sometimes to ask of those who hear what it is that they ought to wish demonstrated to them, in this manner: "This we have taught, this we have made plain." So at the same time the hearer's memory will return, and he will think there is nothing besides which he ought to require.

99. And in these kinds, as has been said before, one ought sometimes to go over one's arguments separately, sometimes—which is more artful—to join one's own with the contrary ones; and when you have stated your own argument, then to show how you have dissolved what was brought against it. So by a brief comparison the hearer's memory of both the confirmation and the refutation will be renewed. And these things one ought to vary by other modes of delivery too. For sometimes you may recapitulate in your own person, so as to remind what and in what place you have said each thing; sometimes you may introduce some person or thing and assign the whole recapitulation to it. A person, in this manner: "For if the framer of the law should arise and ask of you thus why you hesitate—what could you say, when this and this has been demonstrated to you?" And here, as in our own person, it will be possible at one time to go over all the arguments singly, at another to refer them to the several kinds of the partition, at another to ask of the hearer what he requires, at another to do these things by comparison of one's own and the contrary arguments.

100. A thing will be introduced if the speech is assigned, by way of recapitulation, to some object of this kind—a law, a place, a city, a monument—in this manner: "What? If the laws could speak, would they not make this complaint before you: 'What more do you require, judges, when this and this has been made plain to you?'" In this kind too it will be possible to use all the same modes. And this common precept is given for recapitulation: that from each several argument, since the whole cannot be stated again, that be chosen which is weightiest, and each single point be passed over as briefly as possible, so that the memory, not the speech, may seem to be renewed. Indignation is a passage by which it is brought about that great hatred is stirred up against some man, or grave offence against some matter. In this kind we wish it first to be understood that indignation can be handled from all those topics which we have set down in the precept on confirmation. For from those things which are assigned to persons or to actions, any amplifications and indignations can arise; but nevertheless let us consider those things which can be taught separately about indignation.

101. The first topic is taken from authority, when we mention how great a concern that matter was to those whose authority ought to be weightiest: to the immortal gods—which topic is taken from lots, from oracles, soothsayers, portents, prodigies, responses, and the like; likewise to our ancestors, kings, states, nations, the wisest men, the senate, the people, the framers of laws. The second topic is that by which it is shown, with amplification through indignation, to whom that matter pertains—whether to all, or to the greater part, which is most atrocious; or to our superiors, such as those from whose authority the indignation is taken, which is most unworthy; or to those equal to us in spirit, fortune, body, which is most unfair; or to inferiors, which is most arrogant. The third topic is that by which we ask what would come about if others should do the same; and at the same time we show that, if this be granted to this man, there will be many imitators of the same audacity;

102. from which we shall demonstrate what evil will come about. The fourth topic is that by which we show that many are eagerly awaiting what shall be decided, so that from what is granted to one, they may understand what is permitted to themselves too in such a matter. The fifth topic is that by which we show that other matters wrongly settled can, when the truth is understood, be changed and corrected; but that this is a matter which, if it be once judged, can neither be changed by another judgment nor corrected by any power. The sixth topic is that by which it is demonstrated that the deed was done deliberately and of set purpose, and this is added: that pardon ought not to be granted for a voluntary crime, while it is sometimes fitting to make concession to imprudence. The seventh topic is that by which we feel indignation, saying that the deed was foul, cruel, wicked, tyrannical—done by force,

103. by violence, by wealth; a thing most remote from the laws and from equal justice. The eighth topic is that by which we demonstrate that the crime under discussion is not common, nor wont to be committed even by the most audacious men; and that it is remote even from savage men and barbarous nations and monstrous beasts. These will be the things said to have been done cruelly against parents, children, spouses, blood-relations, suppliants; and next, if any such things are brought forward against elders, against guests, against neighbours, against friends, against those with whom one has spent one's life, against those among whom one was brought up, against those by whom one was educated, against the dead, against the wretched and those deserving pity, against famous men, the noble and those who have held honours, against those who could neither harm another nor defend themselves, such as children, old men, women; from all of which, indignation keenly aroused will be able to stir up the greatest hatred against him who has violated any of these.

104. The ninth topic is that by which this matter under question is compared with other faults which are agreed to be faults, and thus, by contrast, it is shown how much more atrocious and unworthy is that which is under discussion. The tenth topic is that by which we gather together everything that was done in the performance of the deed and everything that followed after the deed, with indignation and accusation of each single point, and set the matter before the eyes of the one before whom we speak, as vividly as possible in words, so that what is unworthy may seem to him unworthy just as if he had himself been present and seen it before his eyes. The eleventh topic is that by which we show that the deed was done by one by whom it least ought to have been, and by one who, if another were doing it, would have had a duty to prevent it. The twelfth topic is that by which we feel indignation that this has befallen us first, and has never happened to anyone before.

105. The thirteenth topic is when it is shown that insult is joined to injury; by which topic hatred is stirred up against pride and arrogance. The fourteenth topic is that by which we ask of those who hear that they apply our injuries to their own affairs: if it concerns children, that they think of their own children; if women, of their wives; if old men, of their fathers or parents. The fifteenth topic is that by which we say that the things which have befallen us are wont to seem unworthy even to our enemies and foes. And indignation, in general, will be most weightily drawn from these topics.

106. The appeal to pity is a passage seeking the pity of the hearers. In this one must first render the hearer's mind gentle and merciful, that he may the more easily be moved by the appeal. This must be done by those commonplaces through which the power of fortune over all men and the weakness of mankind are shown; and when such a passage is delivered weightily and sententiously, the spirit of men is greatly humbled and disposed to pity, when in another's misfortune it considers its own weakness.

107. Then the first topic of pity is that by which it is shown in what blessings men have been and in what evils they now are. The second, which is distributed according to times, is that by which it is demonstrated in what evils they have been, and are, and will be. The third is that by which each single misfortune is lamented, as in the death of a son the delight of his boyhood, love, hope, comfort, his upbringing, and whatever can be said by way of appeal in any like kind of misfortune. The fourth is that by which base, lowly, and ignoble things are set forth, and things unworthy of one's age, birth, former fortune, honour, or services, which they have suffered or are about to suffer. The fifth is that by which all the misfortunes are set, one by one, before the eyes, so that he who hears may seem to see, and may be led to pity by the very fact itself, as if he were present, not by words alone.

108. The sixth is that by which it is shown that one is in misery beyond all expectation, and that, when one was expecting something, one not only did not attain it but fell into the greatest miseries. The seventh is that by which we turn to those very ones who hear, and ask that, when they see us, they remember their own children or parents or someone who ought to be dear to them. The eighth is that by which it is said that something was done which ought not to have been, or not done which ought to have been, in this manner: "I was not present, I did not see, I did not hear his last word, I did not receive his last breath." Likewise: "He died in the hands of his enemies, he lay disgracefully unburied in a hostile land, long mangled by wild beasts; in death he was deprived even of the common honour."

109. The ninth is that by which the speech is referred to mute and inanimate things, as if you should adapt to a horse, a house, a garment the words of someone, by which the spirit of those who hear and have loved someone is greatly moved. The tenth is that by which want, weakness, and loneliness are demonstrated. The eleventh is that by which a charge is made to bury one's children or parents or one's own body, or some matter of that kind. The twelfth is that by which separation from someone is lamented, when you are parted from one with whom you most gladly lived, as a parent from a son, a brother from a close friend. The thirteenth is that by which we complain with indignation that we are ill-treated by those by whom it least befits—by kinsmen, friends, to whom we have done kindness, whom we thought would be our helpers; or that we are ill-treated by those by whom it is unworthy—by slaves, freedmen, clients, suppliants. The fourteenth is that which is taken by way of entreaty, in which those who hear are merely begged, in humble and suppliant speech, to feel pity. The fifteenth is that by which we show that we lament not our own fortunes, but those of those who ought to be dear to us. The sixteenth is that by which we show that our own spirit is merciful toward others, and yet that it is great and lofty and patient of misfortunes, and will be so, if anything should happen; for often virtue and magnificence, in which there is gravity and authority, avail more to stir pity than humility and entreaty. But when their spirits have been moved, one ought not to linger longer in the appeal to pity. For, as the rhetorician Apollonius said, nothing dries more quickly than a tear. But since we seem to have said enough about all the parts of the speech, and the size of this volume has proceeded rather far, what follows next we shall say in the second book.
